chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Distance and Displacement
chunks.text:
**Distance** is the total path length traveled by an object. It is a scalar quantity.

**Displacement** is the change in position of an object. It is a vector quantity with both magnitude and direction.

**Key Differences:**
- Distance ≥ |Displacement| always
- Distance is always positive, displacement can be negative
- For straight line motion in one direction: Distance = |Displacement|

**Formula:**
Displacement Δx = x₂ - x₁
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Distance and Displacement

chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Speed and Velocity
chunks.text:
**Speed** is the rate of change of distance traveled. It is a scalar.
- Average speed = Total distance / Total time
- Instantaneous speed = |dx/dt|

**Velocity** is the rate of change of displacement. It is a vector.
- Average velocity = Displacement / Time = Δx/Δt
- Instantaneous velocity = dx/dt

**Key Points:**
- Speed is always positive
- Velocity can be positive or negative
- Average speed ≥ |Average velocity|
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Speed and Velocity

chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Acceleration
chunks.text:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

**Formulas:**
- Average acceleration: a_avg = Δv/Δt = (v - u)/t
- Instantaneous acceleration: a = dv/dt = d²x/dt²

**Sign Convention:**
- Positive acceleration: velocity increasing in positive direction
- Negative acceleration (deceleration): velocity decreasing
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Acceleration

chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Equations of Motion (SUVAT)
chunks.text:
For uniformly accelerated motion (constant acceleration):

**First Equation (Velocity-Time):**
v = u + at

**Second Equation (Displacement-Time):**
s = ut + ½at²

**Third Equation (Velocity-Displacement):**
v² = u² + 2as

**Average Velocity Method:**
s = ((u + v)/2) × t

where:
- u = initial velocity (m/s)
- v = final velocity (m/s)
- a = acceleration (m/s²)
- t = time (s)
- s = displacement (m)

**Common Mistakes:**
1. Using these equations for non-uniform acceleration
2. Sign errors with direction
3. Confusing distance with displacement
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Equations of Motion (SUVAT)

chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Free Fall Motion
chunks.text:
Motion under gravity alone (air resistance negligible).

**Key Facts:**
- g = 9.8 m/s² (or 10 m/s² for approximation)
- g is positive downward (convention)
- All objects fall with same acceleration regardless of mass

**Equations for free fall:**
- v = u + gt (downward positive)
- h = ut + ½gt²
- v² = u² + 2gh

**For upward throw:**
- Use g = -9.8 m/s² (negative)
- Time to reach max height: t = u/g
- Max height: H = u²/2g
- Time of flight: T = 2u/g
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Free Fall Motion

chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Relative Motion
chunks.text:
**Relative Velocity:**
Velocity of A relative to B: v_AB = v_A - v_B

**Key Applications:**
1. Two objects moving in same direction: v_rel = |v₁ - v₂|
2. Two objects moving in opposite directions: v_rel = |v₁ + v₂|
3. Rain and umbrella problems
4. River crossing problems
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Relative Motion

chunks.section: Ch3 Motion In Straight Line > Graphical Analysis
chunks.text:
**Displacement-Time (x-t) Graph:**
- Slope = velocity
- Straight line = constant velocity
- Curve = changing velocity
- Horizontal line = at rest

**Velocity-Time (v-t) Graph:**
- Slope = acceleration
- Area under curve = displacement
- Straight line = constant acceleration
- Horizontal line = constant velocity

**Acceleration-Time (a-t) Graph:**
- Area under curve = change in velocity
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Straight Line, Graphical Analysis

chunks.section: Ch4 Motion In Plane > Scalar and Vector Quantities
chunks.text:
**Scalars:** Have magnitude only (mass, time, speed, distance, temperature)

**Vectors:** Have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force)

**Vector Notation:**
- Bold letter: **A** or arrow notation: Ā
- Magnitude: |A| or A
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Plane, Scalar and Vector Quantities

chunks.section: Ch4 Motion In Plane > Vector Addition and Subtraction
chunks.text:
**Triangle Law:** Place vectors head-to-tail, resultant joins tail of first to head of last.

**Parallelogram Law:** Two vectors from same point form parallelogram, diagonal is resultant.

**Resultant of Two Vectors:**
R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)

Direction: tan α = (B sin θ)/(A + B cos θ)

**Special Cases:**
- θ = 0° (same direction): R = A + B
- θ = 180° (opposite): R = |A - B|
- θ = 90° (perpendicular): R = √(A² + B²)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Plane, Vector Addition and Subtraction

chunks.section: Ch4 Motion In Plane > Resolution of Vectors
chunks.text:
Any vector can be resolved into components:

**In 2D:**
- Aₓ = A cos θ (horizontal component)
- Aᵧ = A sin θ (vertical component)
- A = √(Aₓ² + Aᵧ²)
- θ = tan⁻¹(Aᵧ/Aₓ)

**Unit Vectors:**
- î (along x-axis)
- ĵ (along y-axis)
- k̂ (along z-axis)

A = Aₓî + Aᵧĵ + Aᵤk̂
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Plane, Resolution of Vectors

chunks.section: Ch4 Motion In Plane > Projectile Motion
chunks.text:
Motion of object thrown at an angle to horizontal under gravity.

**Key Assumptions:**
- Air resistance negligible
- g is constant and downward
- Earth's curvature ignored

**Equations (θ = angle of projection, u = initial speed):**

**Time of Flight:**
T = 2u sin θ / g

**Maximum Height:**
H = u² sin² θ / 2g

**Horizontal Range:**
R = u² sin 2θ / g

**Maximum Range:** At θ = 45°, R_max = u²/g

**Key Points:**
- Horizontal velocity remains constant: uₓ = u cos θ
- Vertical velocity changes: vᵧ = u sin θ - gt
- Trajectory is parabolic
- Range is same for θ and (90° - θ)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Plane, Projectile Motion

chunks.section: Ch4 Motion In Plane > Uniform Circular Motion
chunks.text:
Motion in a circle at constant speed.

**Key Facts:**
- Speed is constant but velocity changes direction
- Acceleration is centripetal (toward center)
- Velocity is always tangent to circle

**Centripetal Acceleration:**
aᶜ = v²/r = ω²r

**Centripetal Force:**
Fᶜ = mv²/r = mω²r

**Angular Quantities:**
- Angular velocity: ω = 2π/T = 2πf (rad/s)
- Time period: T = 2πr/v
- Frequency: f = 1/T

**Common Mistakes:**
1. Calling centripetal force as "centrifugal"
2. Forgetting that centripetal force is not a new force
3. Not recognizing circular motion in problems
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Plane, Uniform Circular Motion

chunks.section: Ch4 Motion In Plane > Relative Velocity in 2D
chunks.text:
**Rain-Umbrella Problem:**
- Rain appears to come at angle
- v_rain_relative = v_rain - v_person
- Tilt umbrella in direction of relative velocity

**River Crossing:**
- To cross shortest path: swim at angle upstream
- To cross in minimum time: swim perpendicular to flow
- Drift = (velocity of river) × (time to cross)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Motion in a Plane, Relative Velocity in 2D

chunks.section: Ch5 Laws Of Motion > Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia)
chunks.text:
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.

**Key Points:**
- Inertia is the property of matter that resists changes in motion
- Mass is a measure of inertia - more mass means more inertia
- This law defines the concept of force as something that changes motion

**Examples:**
1. A book on a table remains at rest until pushed
2. A rolling ball eventually stops due to friction (an external force)
3. Passengers lurch forward when a bus stops suddenly

**Formula:** No specific formula, but leads to the concept: F = 0 implies Δv = 0
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Laws of Motion, Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia)

chunks.section: Ch5 Laws Of Motion > Newton's Second Law (F = ma)
chunks.text:
The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts.

**Mathematical Form:**
F = ma = m(dv/dt) = dp/dt

where:
- F = Force (Newtons, N)
- m = Mass (kg)
- a = Acceleration (m/s²)
- p = Momentum (kg·m/s)

**Key Points:**
- Force and acceleration are vectors - direction matters
- 1 Newton = force needed to accelerate 1 kg by 1 m/s²
- Weight W = mg is a special case where a = g

**Problem Solving Approach:**
1. Draw free body diagram
2. Choose coordinate system
3. Write F = ma for each direction
4. Solve equations
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Laws of Motion, Newton's Second Law (F = ma)

chunks.section: Ch5 Laws Of Motion > Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction)
chunks.text:
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When one body exerts a force on another body, the second body simultaneously exerts a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction on the first body.

**Key Points:**
- Action and reaction act on DIFFERENT bodies
- They are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction
- They occur simultaneously
- They do NOT cancel out (because they act on different objects)

**Examples:**
1. When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you
2. Rocket propulsion: gases push rocket up, rocket pushes gases down
3. Walking: you push ground backward, ground pushes you forward

**Common Misconception:** "Action and reaction cancel out" - FALSE! They act on different bodies.
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Laws of Motion, Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction)

chunks.text:
Friction is the force that opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact.

**Types of Friction:**
1. **Static Friction (fs):** Prevents motion from starting
   - fs ≤ μs × N (maximum value)
   - Always equal and opposite to applied force (up to maximum)

2. **Kinetic Friction (fk):** Opposes motion when object is moving
   - fk = μk × N (constant value)
   - μk < μs (kinetic coefficient is less than static)

**Formulas:**
- f = μN
- fs(max) = μs × N
- fk = μk × N

where:
- μ = coefficient of friction (dimensionless)
- N = Normal force (N)

**Factors Affecting Friction:**
- Nature of surfaces in contact
- Normal force pressing surfaces together
- NOT dependent on area of contact (for dry friction)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Laws of Motion, Friction

chunks.section: Ch6 Work Energy > Work Done by a Force
chunks.text:
Work is done when a force causes displacement. It is the product of force and displacement in the direction of force.

**Formula:**
W = F · d · cos(θ)

where:
- W = Work done (Joules, J)
- F = Force applied (N)
- d = Displacement (m)
- θ = Angle between force and displacement

**Key Points:**
- Work is a scalar quantity
- 1 Joule = 1 N × 1 m
- Work is positive when force and displacement are in same direction (θ < 90°)
- Work is negative when force opposes displacement (θ > 90°)
- Work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°)

**Examples:**
- Lifting a book: W = mgh (positive work by you)
- Friction on sliding block: W = -μmgd (negative work)
- Normal force: W = 0 (perpendicular to motion)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Work, Energy and Power, Work Done by a Force

chunks.text:
Energy possessed by a body due to its motion.

**Formula:**
KE = ½mv²

where:
- KE = Kinetic energy (J)
- m = Mass (kg)
- v = Velocity (m/s)

**Key Points:**
- Always positive (v² is always positive)
- Depends on reference frame
- Doubles when velocity doubles? No! Quadruples (v² relationship)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Work, Energy and Power, Kinetic Energy

chunks.text:
Energy stored in a body due to its position or configuration.

**Gravitational Potential Energy:**
PE = mgh

where:
- PE = Potential energy (J)
- m = Mass (kg)
- g = Acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s²)
- h = Height above reference (m)

**Key Points:**
- Reference point can be chosen arbitrarily
- Can be positive, negative, or zero depending on reference
- Only changes in PE are physically meaningful
chunks.subject: Physics
formulas: g = Acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s²)
chunks.source_citation: Work, Energy and Power, Potential Energy

chunks.text:
The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

**Formula:**
W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² - ½mu²

**This is powerful because:**
- Avoids dealing with forces directly
- Works even with variable forces
- Connects force-based and energy-based approaches
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Work, Energy and Power, Work-Energy Theorem

chunks.section: Ch6 Work Energy > Conservation of Energy
chunks.text:
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

**For conservative forces:**
Total Energy = KE + PE = constant

**Formula:**
½mv₁² + mgh₁ = ½mv₂² + mgh₂

**Conservative Forces:** Gravity, spring force, electrostatic force
**Non-conservative Forces:** Friction, air resistance
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Work, Energy and Power, Conservation of Energy

chunks.text:
Rate of doing work or rate of energy transfer.

**Formulas:**
P = W/t = F · v

where:
- P = Power (Watts, W)
- W = Work done (J)
- t = Time (s)
- F = Force (N)
- v = Velocity (m/s)

**Units:**
- 1 Watt = 1 J/s
- 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Work, Energy and Power, Power

chunks.section: Ch7 Gravitation > Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
chunks.text:
**Statement:**
Every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

**Formula:**
F = G(m₁m₂)/r²

where:
- G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² (Universal Gravitational Constant)
- m₁, m₂ = masses
- r = distance between centers

**Vector Form:**
F₁₂ = -G(m₁m₂/r²)r̂₁₂

(Negative sign indicates attractive force)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

chunks.section: Ch7 Gravitation > Acceleration Due to Gravity
chunks.text:
**At Earth's Surface:**
g = GM/R²

where:
- M = mass of Earth (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)
- R = radius of Earth (6.37 × 10⁶ m)
- g ≈ 9.8 m/s²

**Variation with Height:**
g_h = g(R/(R+h))² ≈ g(1 - 2h/R) for h << R

**Variation with Depth:**
g_d = g(1 - d/R)

At center (d = R): g = 0

**Variation with Latitude:**
g_φ = g - Rω²cos²φ

At poles (φ = 90°): g maximum
At equator (φ = 0°): g minimum
chunks.subject: Physics
formulas: h = g(R/(R+h))² ≈ g(1 - 2h/R) for h << R
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Acceleration Due to Gravity

chunks.text:
**Definition:**
Work done to bring mass from infinity to point.

**Formula:**
U = -GMm/r

**Key Points:**
- Always negative (bound system)
- Zero at infinity
- U increases (becomes less negative) as r increases

**Near Earth's Surface:**
U = mgh (with surface as reference)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Gravitational Potential Energy

chunks.text:
**Definition:**
Potential energy per unit mass.

**Formula:**
V = -GM/r

**Units:** J/kg or m²/s²

**Relation:**
g = -dV/dr
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Gravitational Potential

chunks.text:
**Definition:**
Minimum velocity to escape Earth's gravitational field.

**Formula:**
v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR)

For Earth: v_e ≈ 11.2 km/s

**Derivation:**
KE at surface = PE gained to reach infinity
½mv_e² = GMm/R
chunks.subject: Physics
formulas: e = PE gained to reach infinity
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Escape Velocity

chunks.text:
**For circular orbit at height h:**
v_o = √(GM/(R+h)) = √(gR²/(R+h))

**Near surface:** v_o = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s

**Relation with escape velocity:**
v_e = √2 × v_o
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Orbital Velocity

chunks.text:
**Time Period:**
T = 2π√((R+h)³/GM) = 2π√((R+h)³/(gR²))

**Kepler's Third Law:**
T² ∝ r³

**Energy of Satellite:**
- KE = GMm/2r = ½mv_o²
- PE = -GMm/r
- Total E = -GMm/2r = -KE

**Geostationary Satellite:**
- Period = 24 hours
- Height ≈ 36,000 km
- Above equator, moves with Earth
- Used for communication
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Satellite Motion

chunks.section: Ch7 Gravitation > Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
chunks.text:
**First Law (Law of Orbits):**
Planets move in elliptical orbits with Sun at one focus.

**Second Law (Law of Areas):**
Line joining planet and Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times.
(Conservation of angular momentum)

**Third Law (Law of Periods):**
T² ∝ a³

where a = semi-major axis of ellipse

T²/a³ = 4π²/(GM)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion

chunks.text:
**Apparent Weight:**
W_apparent = m(g - a)

**True Weightlessness:**
- At center of Earth (g = 0)
- In deep space (no gravitational field)

**Apparent Weightlessness:**
- In free fall (a = g)
- In orbiting satellite (centripetal acceleration = g)
- At neutral point between Earth and Moon
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Weightlessness

chunks.text:
**Definition:**
Energy required to remove satellite from orbit to infinity.

**Formula:**
BE = -E = GMm/2r = ½mv_o²

**To escape from orbit:**
Need additional energy = GMm/2r
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Gravitation, Binding Energy

chunks.text:
Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter that causes it to experience a force in an electric field.

**Properties:**
- Two types: positive and negative
- Like charges repel, unlike charges attract
- Charge is conserved (total charge in isolated system is constant)
- Charge is quantized: q = ne (n = integer, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

**SI Unit:** Coulomb (C)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electric Charges and Fields, Electric Charge

chunks.text:
The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

**Formula:**
F = k × q₁ × q₂ / r²

where:
- F = Force (N)
- k = Coulomb's constant = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²
- q₁, q₂ = Charges (C)
- r = Distance between charges (m)

**Vector Form:**
F₁₂ = k × q₁ × q₂ × r̂₁₂ / r²

**Key Points:**
- Inverse square law (like gravity)
- Acts along the line joining the charges
- Force is attractive for unlike charges, repulsive for like charges
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electric Charges and Fields, Coulomb's Law

chunks.text:
Electric field is the region around a charge where another charge experiences a force.

**Definition:**
E = F / q₀

where q₀ is a small positive test charge.

**For a Point Charge:**
E = k × Q / r²

**Key Points:**
- Vector quantity - has magnitude and direction
- Direction: away from positive charge, toward negative charge
- Field lines never cross
- Closer field lines = stronger field

**Electric Field Lines Properties:**
1. Start from positive charges, end on negative charges
2. Never cross each other
3. Perpendicular to conductor surface
4. Density indicates field strength
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electric Charges and Fields, Electric Field

chunks.text:
Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge to bring a charge from infinity to that point.

**Formula:**
V = k × Q / r

where:
- V = Electric potential (Volts, V)
- Q = Source charge (C)
- r = Distance from charge (m)

**Potential Difference:**
V_AB = V_A - V_B = W_AB / q

**Relation to Electric Field:**
E = -dV/dr

**Key Points:**
- Scalar quantity (easier to work with than E)
- Potential due to multiple charges = algebraic sum
- Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electric Charges and Fields, Electric Potential

chunks.text:
Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.

**Formula:**
I = Q/t = dQ/dt

**Units:** Ampere (A) = Coulomb/second

**Direction:** Conventional current flows from positive to negative (opposite to electron flow)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Electric Current

chunks.section: Ch2 Current Electricity > Drift Velocity and Current
chunks.text:
**Drift Velocity:** Average velocity of electrons in a conductor due to applied field.

**Formula:**
vd = eEτ/m = I/(neA)

where:
- e = electron charge (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
- E = electric field
- τ = relaxation time
- m = electron mass
- n = number density of electrons
- A = cross-sectional area

**Current Density:**
J = I/A = nevd = σE
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Drift Velocity and Current

chunks.text:
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature.

**Formula:**
V = IR

where:
- V = potential difference (Volts)
- I = current (Amperes)
- R = resistance (Ohms)

**Ohmic Conductors:** Follow Ohm's law (metals at constant temperature)
**Non-ohmic Conductors:** Don't follow (diodes, transistors)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Ohm's Law

chunks.section: Ch2 Current Electricity > Resistance and Resistivity
chunks.text:
**Resistance:**
R = ρL/A

where:
- ρ = resistivity (Ω·m)
- L = length
- A = cross-sectional area

**Conductivity:** σ = 1/ρ

**Temperature Dependence (metals):**
R_T = R₀(1 + αT)
ρ_T = ρ₀(1 + αT)

where α = temperature coefficient of resistance
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Resistance and Resistivity

chunks.section: Ch2 Current Electricity > Combination of Resistors
chunks.text:
**Series Connection:**
- Same current through all
- R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...
- V_total = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ + ...

**Parallel Connection:**
- Same voltage across all
- 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + ...
- I_total = I₁ + I₂ + I₃ + ...

**For two resistors in parallel:**
R_eq = (R₁ × R₂)/(R₁ + R₂)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Combination of Resistors

chunks.section: Ch2 Current Electricity > EMF and Internal Resistance
chunks.text:
**EMF (ε):** Work done by cell per unit charge in complete circuit

**Terminal Voltage:**
V = ε - Ir

where r = internal resistance of cell

**In circuit:**
I = ε/(R + r)

**Maximum Power Transfer:**
Occurs when R = r (external = internal resistance)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, EMF and Internal Resistance

chunks.text:
**First Law (Junction Rule):**
Sum of currents entering a junction = Sum of currents leaving
∑I_in = ∑I_out

(Conservation of charge)

**Second Law (Loop Rule):**
Sum of potential differences around any closed loop = 0
∑V = 0

(Conservation of energy)

**Sign Convention:**
- EMF: + if loop goes from - to + terminal
- Resistor: + if loop goes against current direction
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Kirchhoff's Laws

chunks.section: Ch2 Current Electricity > Electrical Power and Energy
chunks.text:
**Power:**
P = VI = I²R = V²/R

**Units:** Watt (W) = Joule/second

**Energy:**
E = Pt = VIt = I²Rt = V²t/R

**Units:** Joule (J), kilowatt-hour (kWh)
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Electrical Power and Energy

chunks.text:
Balanced when no current flows through galvanometer.

**Balance Condition:**
P/Q = R/S

or equivalently: PS = QR

**Applications:**
- Measurement of unknown resistance
- Meter bridge (slide wire bridge)
- Post office box
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Current Electricity, Wheatstone Bridge

chunks.text:
Magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force is experienced by moving charges.

**Magnetic Field Lines:**
- Form closed loops (no magnetic monopoles)
- Direction: from North to South outside magnet
- Never intersect
- Closer lines = stronger field

**Units:** Tesla (T) = Wb/m² = N/(A·m)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Magnetic Field

chunks.text:
Magnetic field due to a current element.

**Formula:**
dB = (μ₀/4π) × (I dl × r̂)/r²

where:
- μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A (permeability of free space)
- I = current
- dl = length element
- r = distance from element

**Field at Center of Circular Loop:**
B = μ₀I/2R

**Field on Axis of Circular Loop:**
B = μ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Biot-Savart Law

chunks.text:
**Statement:**
∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed

The line integral of B around a closed loop equals μ₀ times the current enclosed.

**Applications:**

**Infinite Straight Wire:**
B = μ₀I/(2πr)

**Solenoid:**
B = μ₀nI (inside)
B ≈ 0 (outside)

where n = N/L = number of turns per unit length

**Toroid:**
B = μ₀NI/(2πr) (inside)
B = 0 (outside)
chunks.subject: Physics
formulas: n = N/L = number of turns per unit length
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Ampere's Circuital Law

chunks.section: Ch3 Magnetism > Force on Moving Charge (Lorentz Force)
chunks.text:
**Magnetic Force:**
F = qv × B

Magnitude: F = qvB sin θ

**Direction:** Use right-hand rule

**Key Points:**
- Force is perpendicular to both v and B
- Force does no work (doesn't change KE)
- Charge moves in circular path if v ⊥ B

**Radius of circular path:**
r = mv/(qB)

**Time period:**
T = 2πm/(qB) (independent of velocity!)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Force on Moving Charge (Lorentz Force)

chunks.section: Ch3 Magnetism > Force on Current-Carrying Conductor
chunks.text:
**Formula:**
F = IL × B

Magnitude: F = BIL sin θ

**Direction:** Right-hand rule
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Force on Current-Carrying Conductor

chunks.section: Ch3 Magnetism > Force Between Parallel Currents
chunks.text:
**Two parallel wires:**
F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)

**Direction:**
- Same direction currents: Attract
- Opposite direction currents: Repel

**Definition of Ampere:**
1 A is the current which, when flowing through two parallel infinite wires 1 m apart, produces force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N/m.
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Force Between Parallel Currents

chunks.section: Ch3 Magnetism > Torque on Current Loop
chunks.text:
A current loop in a magnetic field experiences a torque.

**Torque:**
τ = NBIA sin θ = M × B

where:
- N = number of turns
- B = magnetic field
- I = current
- A = area of loop
- M = NIA = magnetic moment

**Potential Energy:**
U = -M·B = -MB cos θ

**Stable equilibrium:** θ = 0 (M parallel to B)
**Unstable equilibrium:** θ = 180° (M antiparallel to B)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Torque on Current Loop

chunks.text:
**Principle:** Torque on current loop in magnetic field

**Deflection:**
θ = (NAB/k) × I

where k = torsional constant of spring

**Current Sensitivity:** θ/I = NAB/k
**Voltage Sensitivity:** θ/V = NAB/(kR)

**Conversion to Ammeter:**
Add low resistance (shunt) S in parallel
S = Ig × G/(I - Ig)

**Conversion to Voltmeter:**
Add high resistance R in series
R = V/Ig - G
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current, Moving Coil Galvanometer

chunks.text:
Magnetic flux is the number of magnetic field lines passing through a surface.

**Formula:**
Φ = B·A = BA cos θ

where θ = angle between B and normal to surface

**Units:** Weber (Wb) = T·m²
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Magnetic Flux

chunks.section: Ch4 Electromagnetic Induction > Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction
chunks.text:
**First Law:**
Whenever magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an EMF is induced.

**Second Law:**
The induced EMF is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux.

**Formula:**
ε = -dΦ/dt

For N turns: ε = -N(dΦ/dt)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction

chunks.text:
The induced current flows in a direction such that it opposes the change that produces it.

**Applications:**
- Conservation of energy
- Determines direction of induced current
- Explains the negative sign in Faraday's law

**Examples:**
- Magnet approaching coil: induced current creates repelling field
- Magnet receding: induced current creates attracting field
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Lenz's Law

chunks.text:
EMF induced in a conductor moving through a magnetic field.

**For rod of length L moving with velocity v perpendicular to B:**
ε = BLv

**General form:**
ε = ∮(v × B)·dl

**Direction:** Use right-hand rule or Lenz's law
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Motional EMF

chunks.text:
Induced currents in bulk conductors when flux changes.

**Effects:**
- Heating (I²R losses)
- Damping of motion
- Electromagnetic braking

**Applications:**
- Induction heating
- Electric brakes
- Speedometers
- Induction cookers

**Reduction:** Use laminated cores to reduce path for eddy currents
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Eddy Currents

chunks.text:
Property of a coil that opposes change in current through it.

**Self-induced EMF:**
ε = -L(dI/dt)

where L = self-inductance (Henry, H)

**Inductance of Solenoid:**
L = μ₀n²AL = μ₀N²A/L

where:
- n = N/L = turns per unit length
- A = cross-sectional area
- L = length of solenoid

**Energy Stored in Inductor:**
U = ½LI²
chunks.subject: Physics
formulas: n = N/L = turns per unit length
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Self-Inductance

chunks.text:
Flux linkage in one coil due to current in another.

**Mutual induced EMF:**
ε₂ = -M(dI₁/dt)

**For two solenoids:**
M = μ₀n₁n₂AL

**Coefficient of Coupling:**
k = M/√(L₁L₂)

For perfect coupling: k = 1, M = √(L₁L₂)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Mutual Inductance

chunks.text:
Converts mechanical energy to electrical energy.

**Principle:** Electromagnetic induction

**EMF produced:**
ε = ε₀ sin(ωt)

where ε₀ = NABω = peak EMF

**Average EMF (half cycle):** ε_avg = 2ε₀/π

**RMS EMF:** ε_rms = ε₀/√2

chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, AC Generator

chunks.text:
Transfers electrical energy between circuits through mutual induction.

**Transformation Ratio:**
N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p = I_p/I_s

**Step-up:** N_s > N_p (increases voltage)
**Step-down:** N_s < N_p (decreases voltage)

**Efficiency:**
η = (Output power)/(Input power) × 100%

**Energy Losses:**
1. Copper losses (I²R in windings)
2. Iron losses (eddy currents, hysteresis)
3. Flux leakage
4. Magnetostriction
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Electromagnetic Induction, Transformer

chunks.text:
**Laws of Reflection:**
1. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in same plane
2. Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (i = r)

**Plane Mirror:**
- Image is virtual, erect, same size
- Image distance = Object distance
- Lateral inversion occurs

**Spherical Mirrors:**

**Mirror Formula:**
1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R

**Magnification:**
m = -v/u = h'/h

**Sign Convention (New Cartesian):**
- Distances measured from pole
- Along incident light: positive
- Against incident light: negative
- Above principal axis: positive
- Below principal axis: negative
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, Reflection of Light

chunks.text:
**Laws of Refraction:**
1. Incident ray, refracted ray, normal lie in same plane
2. Snell's Law: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r

**Refractive Index:**
n = c/v = (speed in vacuum)/(speed in medium)

**Relative Refractive Index:**
n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂ = λ₁/λ₂
chunks.subject: Physics
formulas: n = c/v = (speed in vacuum)/(speed in medium)
chunks.source_citation: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, Refraction of Light

chunks.text:
Occurs when light goes from denser to rarer medium at angle > critical angle.

**Critical Angle:**
sin C = n₂/n₁ (where n₂ < n₁)

**Conditions:**
1. Light must travel from denser to rarer medium
2. Angle of incidence > Critical angle

**Applications:**
- Optical fibers
- Prisms in binoculars
- Diamond brilliance
- Mirages
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, Total Internal Reflection

chunks.text:
**Lens Maker's Equation:**
1/f = (n - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂)

**Thin Lens Formula:**
1/v - 1/u = 1/f

**Magnification:**
m = v/u = h'/h

**Power of Lens:**
P = 1/f (in meters)

Units: Diopter (D)

**Combination of Lenses (in contact):**
1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + ...
P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, Thin Lens Formula

chunks.text:
**Deviation:**
δ = i + e - A

where A = angle of prism

**Minimum Deviation:**
At minimum deviation: i = e, r₁ = r₂ = A/2

**Formula for n:**
n = sin[(A + δₘ)/2] / sin(A/2)

**Dispersion:**
Different wavelengths refract differently
n_violet > n_red
δ_violet > δ_red

**Angular Dispersion:**
θ = δ_v - δ_r = (n_v - n_r)A

**Dispersive Power:**
ω = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)
chunks.subject: Physics
chunks.source_citation: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, Prism

chunks.text:
**Simple Microscope:**
Magnifying power: M = 1 + D/f (for image at D)
M = D/f (for image at infinity)

where D = 25 cm (least distance of distinct vision)

**Compound Microscope:**
M = m_o × m_e = (L/f_o) × (D/f_e)

**Telescope (Astronomical):**
M = f_o/f_e (for image at infinity)
Length = f_o + f_e

**Resolving Power:**

Microscope: RP = 2n sin θ/λ

Telescope: RP = D/1.22λ
